claim: In the United States in 2019, only 16% of scientists and engineers were women.
source: In the United States in 2019, for example, only 16% of scientists and engineers were women (National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics, 2021

claim: Women are underrepresented across all professorship ranks.
source: Women are also underrepresented across all professorship ranks (Chesler et al., 2010; Mason et al., 2013), especially among full professors – in 2018 only 32.5% of full professors in the United States were women (Colby and Fowler, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chesler et al., 2010; Mason et al., 2013; and Colby and Fowler, 2020

claim: In 2018 only 32.5% of full professors in the United States were women.
source: Women are also underrepresented across all professorship ranks (Chesler et al., 2010; Mason et al., 2013), especially among full professors – in 2018 only 32.5% of full professors in the United States were women (Colby and Fowler, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Colby and Fowler, 2020

claim: Women academics produce fewer papers compared with men.
source: Studies show that, compared with men, women academics produce fewer papers (Larivière et al., 2013; Paul-Hus et al., 2015), receive fewer citations (Caplar et al., 2017; Maliniak et al., 2013), and have narrower collaboration networks (Ductor et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Larivière et al., 2013 and Paul-Hus et al., 2015

claim: Women academics receive fewer citations compared with men.
source: Studies show that, compared with men, women academics produce fewer papers (Larivière et al., 2013; Paul-Hus et al., 2015), receive fewer citations (Caplar et al., 2017; Maliniak et al., 2013), and have narrower collaboration networks (Ductor et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caplar et al., 2017 and Maliniak et al., 2013

claim: Women academics have narrower collaboration networks compared with men.
source: Studies show that, compared with men, women academics produce fewer papers (Larivière et al., 2013; Paul-Hus et al., 2015), receive fewer citations (Caplar et al., 2017; Maliniak et al., 2013), and have narrower collaboration networks (Ductor et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ductor et al., 2021

claim: Women are less likely to receive project funding.
source: Women are also less likely to receive project funding (Ley and Hamilton, 2008; Witteman et al., 2019) or prestigious awards (Lunnemann et al., 2019; Meho, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ley and Hamilton, 2008 and Witteman et al., 2019

claim: Women are less likely to receive prestigious awards.
source: Women are also less likely to receive project funding (Ley and Hamilton, 2008; Witteman et al., 2019) or prestigious awards (Lunnemann et al., 2019; Meho, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lunnemann et al., 2019 and Meho, 2021

claim: Gendered differences in academia are usually correlated and mutually reinforcing, contributing to lower career satisfaction and higher attrition rates for women in academia.
source: These gendered differences are usually correlated and mutually reinforcing, contributing to lower career satisfaction and higher attrition rates for women in academia (Xu, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu, 2008

claim: Parenting is considered highly related to gender disparities in academia.
source: Parenting is considered highly related to gender disparities in academia (Hunter and Leahey, 2010; Kelly and Grant, 2012; Morgan et al., 2021; Powell, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hunter and Leahey, 2010; Kelly and Grant, 2012; Morgan et al., 2021; and Powell, 2021

claim: Parenting contributes to the gender gap in scientific productivity.
source: It contributes to the gender gap in many key research performance metrics, such as scientific productivity (Mairesse et al., 2019; Morgan et al., 2021), citations (Lawson et al., 2021), and academic collaboration (Hunter and Leahey, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mairesse et al., 2019 and Morgan et al., 2021

claim: Parenting contributes to the gender gap in citations.
source: It contributes to the gender gap in many key research performance metrics, such as scientific productivity (Mairesse et al., 2019; Morgan et al., 2021), citations (Lawson et al., 2021), and academic collaboration (Hunter and Leahey, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lawson et al., 2021

claim: Parenting contributes to the gender gap in academic collaboration.
source: It contributes to the gender gap in many key research performance metrics, such as scientific productivity (Mairesse et al., 2019; Morgan et al., 2021), citations (Lawson et al., 2021), and academic collaboration (Hunter and Leahey, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hunter and Leahey, 2010

claim: Career satisfaction in academia is lower for mothers than fathers.
source: Evidence also shows that career satisfaction in academia is lower for mothers than fathers (Beckett et al., 2015), likely due to the reasons such as limited opportunities for tenure and promotion (Finkel and Olswang, 1996; Mason et al., 2013), lower salary (Kelly and Grant, 2012), and higher levels of work-family conflict (Martins et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beckett et al., 2015

claim: Lower career satisfaction for mothers is likely due to limited opportunities for tenure and promotion.
source: Evidence also shows that career satisfaction in academia is lower for mothers than fathers (Beckett et al., 2015), likely due to the reasons such as limited opportunities for tenure and promotion (Finkel and Olswang, 1996; Mason et al., 2013), lower salary (Kelly and Grant, 2012), and higher levels of work-family conflict (Martins et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Finkel and Olswang, 1996 and Mason et al., 2013

claim: Lower career satisfaction for mothers is likely due to lower salary.
source: Evidence also shows that career satisfaction in academia is lower for mothers than fathers (Beckett et al., 2015), likely due to the reasons such as limited opportunities for tenure and promotion (Finkel and Olswang, 1996; Mason et al., 2013), lower salary (Kelly and Grant, 2012), and higher levels of work-family conflict (Martins et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelly and Grant, 2012

claim: Lower career satisfaction for mothers is likely due to higher levels of work-family conflict.
source: Evidence also shows that career satisfaction in academia is lower for mothers than fathers (Beckett et al., 2015), likely due to the reasons such as limited opportunities for tenure and promotion (Finkel and Olswang, 1996; Mason et al., 2013), lower salary (Kelly and Grant, 2012), and higher levels of work-family conflict (Martins et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martins et al., 2002

claim: The prominent motherhood penalty could impel women to self-select away from academic careers and to leave such careers at higher rates than men.
source: The prominent motherhood penalty could impel women to self-select away from academic careers and to leave such careers at higher rates than men (an effect known as the "leaky pipeline": Anders, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anders, 2004

claim: Work-family conflict can be categorized into three types: time-based conflict, strain-based conflict, and behavior-based conflict.
source: Work-family conflict can be categorized into three types: (i) time-based conflict is the competition of time between different roles, e.g., mother vs. researcher; (ii) strain-based conflict happens when the strain in one role interferes with one's ability to perform in another role; (iii) behavior-based conflict happens when the behavior requirements as a role become incompatible with the behavioral expectation of another (Greenhaus and Beutell, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to Greenhaus and Beutell, 1985

claim: Women usually experience higher levels of work-family conflict than men due to parenting.
source: Studies have indicated that women usually experience higher levels of work-family conflict than men due to parenting (Martins et al., 2002; van Daalen et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2020), and academia is no exception (Fox et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Martins et al., 2002; van Daalen et al., 2006; and Wang et al., 2020

claim: Women in academia experience higher levels of work-family conflict than men due to parenting.
source: Studies have indicated that women usually experience higher levels of work-family conflict than men due to parenting (Martins et al., 2002; van Daalen et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2020), and academia is no exception (Fox et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fox et al., 2011

claim: Mothers who are academics spend more time on childcare responsibilities and household tasks.
source: Mothers who are academics spend more time on childcare responsibilities and household tasks (Misra et al., 2012) and experience more research pressure and job stress than men (van Daalen et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Misra et al., 2012

claim: Mothers who are academics experience more research pressure and job stress than men.
source: Mothers who are academics spend more time on childcare responsibilities and household tasks (Misra et al., 2012) and experience more research pressure and job stress than men (van Daalen et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Daalen et al., 2006

claim: High work-family conflict can significantly affect women's career satisfaction, regardless of their age.
source: It is indicated that high work-family conflict can significantly affect women's career satisfaction, regardless of their age (Martins et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martins et al., 2002

claim: Partner support represents a significant form of family-to-work enrichment and has positive effects.
source: Family support, especially partner support, represents a significant form of family-to-work enrichment and has positive effects (Greenhaus and Powell, 2006; Kinnunen et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Greenhaus and Powell, 2006 and Kinnunen et al., 2006

claim: Partner support can be instrumental or emotional.
source: Partner support can be instrumental or emotional (Adams and Golsch, 2021; Greenhaus and Powell, 2006) and may decrease work turnover rate and boost women's perceptions of gains in productivity and career satisfaction (Ferguson et al., 2016; Juraqulova et al., 2015; Watanabe and Falci, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Adams and Golsch, 2021 and Greenhaus and Powell, 2006

claim: Partner support may decrease work turnover rate and boost women's perceptions of gains in productivity and career satisfaction.
source: Partner support can be instrumental or emotional (Adams and Golsch, 2021; Greenhaus and Powell, 2006) and may decrease work turnover rate and boost women's perceptions of gains in productivity and career satisfaction (Ferguson et al., 2016; Juraqulova et al., 2015; Watanabe and Falci, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferguson et al., 2016; Juraqulova et al., 2015; and Watanabe and Falci, 2016

claim: Partner support can relieve the tension inside the family and reduce the pressure from the family, mitigating work-family conflict and increasing well-being and career performance.
source: Partner support can also relieve the tension inside the family and reduce the pressure from the family, mitigating work-family conflict and increasing well-being and career performance (Dickson, 2020; Ferguson et al., 2016; Thorstad et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dickson, 2020; Ferguson et al., 2016; Thorstad et al., 2006; and Wang et al., 2020

claim: Partner support has been found to help reduce work-family conflict, with the reduction for mothers being greater than that for fathers.
source: Although partner support has been found to help reduce work-family conflict – with the reduction for mothers being greater than that for fathers – the demand for partner support from mothers is often less satisfied (Adams and Golsch, 2021; Dickson, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Adams and Golsch, 2021 and Dickson, 2020

claim: The demand for partner support from mothers is often less satisfied.
source: Although partner support has been found to help reduce work-family conflict – with the reduction for mothers being greater than that for fathers – the demand for partner support from mothers is often less satisfied (Adams and Golsch, 2021; Dickson, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Adams and Golsch, 2021 and Dickson, 2020
